body:
Wisye Sahambangung's journey began in hardship. As a fisher and single woman receiving government social assistance through Indonesia's PKH program, she could have remained dependent on those benefits. Instead, when the local fisheries office invited her to mangrove restoration training in 2022, she seized the opportunity. Today, at 45, she leads Rhizopora, a women's group named after the Rhizophora genus of mangrove trees, which has grown into a thriving conservation and livelihood enterprise transforming Sarawet, a coastal village in North Sulawesi.

The numbers tell the story of what collective effort can achieve. Since its founding, Rhizopora and its partner NGOs planted 30,000 mangrove trees in an eight-month restoration project. Members sell seedlings for 2,500 rupiah each, harvest mud crabs that fetch 350,000 rupiah per kilogram, and operate a savings-and-loans scheme that has enabled one single mother member to purchase a house and launch a small cake business. The group supplies seedlings to major corporations including Alfamidi, a national retail chain, and PLN, the state electricity company. The physical toll was steep—Wisye recalls mud reaching her chest while working coastal areas—but the community-led effort paid off. Local fishers now report catching more fish, evidence that mangrove protection strengthens the ecosystem everyone depends on.

What began as a path out of poverty has become a platform with reach beyond the village. Wisye's work earned her an invitation to speak at an international forum in Australia, her first airplane ride, bringing global attention to Sarawet's model of conservation-led development. Her story challenges the assumption that environmental protection and economic security are competing interests. For the women of Rhizopora, they are inseparable.
